title: Almost hiring Cat Anderson, and Cat's Canadian concert
summary: Barnet chose Al Killian over Cat Anderson on Andy Gibson's advice; years later in Canada in 1973 Cat's premature high notes ruined the buildup.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Oh, he was. You know, there's a little story there. I had told Andy Gibson, I said, "I want a trumpet player, a high note trumpet player, we can use, on the sensational side." He said, "Well, there are two of them, the guy that you liked when you were with Basie, played all the high lead there, and there's a guy here working in town by the name of Cat Anderson." And I said, "Well, who did he play with?" He said, "Well, as far as I know, Sabby Lewis, up in Boston, and I don't think he's played with any name bands or anything like that." And I said, "Well, we'd better go with the experienced. Let's get Al." So I came very close to having Cat.
But Al could play melody up high, higher than Cat can, I think.
Well, Cat is, you know -- Cat can squeeze out notes and everything, but I don't -- he can only play a part up so high, and from then on it's histrionics.

Al was capable of playing, you know, a high lead, on up to an A or something, and the same thing like Maynard Ferguson's capable of doing that. He isn't just a guy that goes up and -- but Cat's a showboat, you know, and he's a jolly little fat man. I love him dearly. I've used him a few times. I went up to Canada here in '73, and I took him up there with me, and I said, "Now, look --," we used the CBC house orchestra up there. We had it one week -- I had it one week, and then Benny Goodman had it one week, and Quincy Jones had it another week. But we were never in residence together. I told Cat, I said, "Look, now, I don't want you to play any high notes until after I introduce you on your number." I said, "Don't blow the show, you know." So he's back there and he's very good, and I finally introduced him, and he's doing that thing he does in the "Birth of the Blues," which of course he picks up all by himself. And I gave him a big buildup in the announcement, you know, so forth and so on,

the greatest lip in the world, and he got up and he, splat, split, splat, splat, da-da, you know, and -- (Laughter) -- the guys in the band broke up. They recovered in time, but he of course acquitted himself nobly after that, but what an awful thing to happen after the buildup, and I had told him, now don't you do anything before you're introduced, because don't blow the game. And then we couldn't keep him out. He was into every arrangement, just playing everybody's parts.
